lead: This unit teaches hypothesis testing: how to decide from sample data whether a claim about a population is supported. You will set null and alternative hypotheses, control type I and type II errors, and use z, t, F and chi-square tests. By the end you can run a test, read a p-value, and report a decision in plain language.
about: This unit turns sample numbers into decisions. Chapter 6.1 sets the language: null and alternative hypotheses, the two error types, significance level and p-value. Chapter 6.2 uses the normal approximation for large samples to test means and proportions. Chapter 6.3 replaces the normal by Student's t when the sample is small and the population standard deviation is unknown. Chapter 6.4 uses the F ratio to compare two variances. Chapter 6.5 uses chi-square for counts: goodness of fit and independence in contingency tables. Chapter 6.6 extends the variance ratio to compare several means by one-way and two-way ANOVA. Each chapter follows the same path: state hypotheses, compute a statistic, compare with a critical value or p-value, and write the decision in context.

chapters.idea: A hypothesis test compares sample evidence with a null model while controlling the chance of a false alarm.
chapters.depth: Define null hypothesis H0 (the claim assumed true) and alternative hypothesis H1 (the claim you want evidence for). One-sided and two-sided alternatives. Test statistic: a number computed from the sample whose distribution is known when H0 is true. Critical region and rejection region. Level of significance α: the chosen maximum probability of rejecting H0 when H0 is true. Type I error: reject a true H0, probability α. Type II error: fail to reject a false H0, probability β. Power = 1 − β. p-value: the smallest α at which the observed statistic would reject H0; for a two-sided test double the one-tailed area. Decision rule: reject H0 if p ≤ α or if the statistic lies in the critical region. Relation to confidence intervals. Some syllabi call α the size of the test and call the rejection region the critical region.

figure.title: Five steps of a test
figure.aria: A vertical flowchart from stating hypotheses to fixing alpha, sampling, computing a statistic, finding a p-value, and deciding.

chapters.example: A battery maker claims a mean life of 1000 h. Test H0: μ = 1000 h against H1: μ < 1000 h at α = 0.05. A sample gives test statistic z = −2.1. The p-value is P(Z ≤ −2.1) = 0.0179. Since 0.0179 < 0.05, reject H0. The sample supports the claim that the mean life is less than 1000 h.
chapters.trap: The p-value is not the probability that H0 is true. α is fixed before looking at the data, and a two-sided p-value doubles the one-tailed area.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (probability) and Unit 5 (sampling distributions, standard error).
chapters.leave: Computing z, t, F and chi-square statistics is done in Chapters 6.2 to 6.6.

chapters.idea: For large samples the central limit theorem makes standardized means and proportions approximately normal, so a z-test gives the decision.
chapters.depth: One-sample mean: z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n), where x̄ is the sample mean, μ0 the claimed mean, σ the population standard deviation and n the sample size. If σ is unknown and n is large, use sample standard deviation s. Two-sample means: z = (x̄1 − x̄2)/√(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2). One proportion: z = (p̂ − p0)/√(p0(1 − p0)/n), where p̂ is the sample proportion and p0 the claimed proportion. Two proportions: pool p̂ = (x1 + x2)/(n1 + n2) and use standard error √(p̂(1 − p̂)(1/n1 + 1/n2)). Large-sample condition n ≥ 30 for means, and np0 ≥ 5 and n(1 − p0) ≥ 5 for proportions; some syllabi use 10 instead of 5. Critical values: 1.96 for a two-sided 5% test, 1.645 for a one-sided 5% test. Confidence interval correspondence.

figure.aria: A standard normal curve with vertical lines at minus 1.96 and plus 1.96 marking the two-tailed 5% rejection region.

chapters.example: A sample of 100 bulbs has mean life 990 h. The population standard deviation is known as 50 h. Test H0: μ = 1000 h against H1: μ ≠ 1000 h at α = 0.05. Standard error = 50/√100 = 5 h. z = (990 − 1000)/5 = −2.0. Since |−2.0| = 2.0 > 1.96, reject H0. The p-value is 0.0455.
chapters.trap: Do not use s in place of σ/√n without checking that n is large. Do not mix one-sided and two-sided critical values.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (normal distribution), Unit 4 (central limit theorem) and Unit 5 (standard error).
chapters.leave: Small-sample tests with unknown σ are in Chapter 6.3; count-data tests are in Chapter 6.5.

chapters.idea: When σ is unknown and the sample is small, the standardized mean follows Student's t with n − 1 degrees of freedom, giving the t-test.
chapters.depth: One-sample t: t = (x̄ − μ0)/(s/√n), with degrees of freedom df = n − 1; s is the sample standard deviation. Two independent samples with pooled variance: s_p² = ((n1 − 1)s1² + (n2 − 1)s2²)/(n1 + n2 − 2), t = (x̄1 − x̄2)/(s_p√(1/n1 + 1/n2)), df = n1 + n2 − 2. Paired t-test: compute differences d, then t = d̄/(s_d/√n), df = n − 1. Assumptions: independent observations and approximately normal populations; for two samples, equal variances when using the pooled form. Welch's unequal-variance t-test is used only by a few universities. Confidence interval: x̄ ± t(α/2, n−1) × s/√n. Some syllabi call this the small-sample t-test or Student's t-test.

figure.aria: A decision tree for choosing a one-sample, two-independent-sample or paired t-test.

chapters.example: A random sample of 10 biscuit packets has mean weight 248 g and sample standard deviation 6 g. The label claims 250 g. Test at α = 0.05 whether the mean is less than 250 g. Standard error = 6/√10 = 1.897 g. t = (248 − 250)/1.897 = −1.054. df = 9. The one-tailed critical value is t(0.05, 9) = 1.833. Since |−1.054| < 1.833, fail to reject H0.
chapters.trap: Use df = n − 1 for one sample and n1 + n2 − 2 for pooled two samples. Do not compare t with a normal critical value when n is small.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 (Student's t distribution and confidence intervals).
chapters.leave: Comparing three or more means is in Chapter 6.6; comparing two variances is in Chapter 6.4.

chapters.idea: The ratio of two independent sample variances follows an F distribution when the populations are normal with equal variances.
chapters.depth: F statistic: F = s1²/s2², where s1² and s2² are sample variances. Degrees of freedom: df1 = n1 − 1 and df2 = n2 − 1. For a one-tailed test H0: σ1² = σ2² against σ1² > σ2², place the larger variance in the numerator and compare with F(α, df1, df2). For a two-tailed test use α/2 and compare with F(α/2, df1, df2), or use a p-value. Assumptions: independent random samples from normal populations. The F distribution was defined in Unit 5. The test is sensitive to non-normality. Some syllabi call it the variance ratio test.

figure.title: Variance ratio test
figure.aria: A flowchart taking two sample variances into an F ratio, comparing it with a critical value, and deciding.

chapters.example: Two machines fill bottles. Machine 1: n1 = 10, s1 = 4.0 ml. Machine 2: n2 = 12, s2 = 2.0 ml. Test H0: σ1² = σ2² against H1: σ1² > σ2² at α = 0.05. F = 4.0²/2.0² = 16/4 = 4.0 with df (9, 11). The critical value is F(0.05, 9, 11) = 2.90. Since 4.0 > 2.90, reject H0; Machine 1 has larger variance.
chapters.trap: For a two-tailed test use α/2 in the F table, not α. Always check the df order (n1 − 1, n2 − 1).
chapters.leave: The same F ratio is used for ANOVA in Chapter 6.6; do not re-derive its distribution there.

chapters.idea: Chi-square tests compare observed counts with expected counts under a model, using squared standardized differences.
chapters.depth: Test statistic: χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E, where O is an observed frequency and E an expected frequency. Goodness of fit: expected frequencies come from a claimed distribution; df = k − 1 − m, where k is the number of categories and m is the number of parameters estimated from the data. Independence in an r × c contingency table: expected count E_ij = (row i total × column j total)/grand total; df = (r − 1)(c − 1). Conditions: expected counts should be at least 5; combine categories if needed. Yates continuity correction for a 2 × 2 table is mentioned in some syllabi. Large values of χ² reject H0. This is the chi-square test of independence or association of attributes.

figure.title: 2×2 contingency table
figure.aria: A two-by-two table of observed counts for coached and not-coached groups with pass, fail and total columns.

chapters.example: A die is rolled 120 times. Counts for faces 1 to 6 are 15, 22, 20, 18, 25, 20. Test fairness at α = 0.05. Expected count = 20 for each face. χ² = (15−20)²/20 + (22−20)²/20 + 0 + (18−20)²/20 + (25−20)²/20 + 0 = 1.25 + 0.20 + 0 + 0.20 + 1.25 + 0 = 2.90. df = 6 − 1 = 5. The critical value is χ²(0.05, 5) = 11.07. Since 2.90 < 11.07, fail to reject fairness.
chapters.trap: The df for independence is (r − 1)(c − 1), not rc − 1. Expected counts must be calculated from table totals, not copied from observed counts.
chapters.leave: Tests on means and variances are in Chapters 6.2 to 6.4; ANOVA is in Chapter 6.6.

chapters.idea: ANOVA splits total variation into between-group and within-group parts and compares their mean squares with an F ratio.
chapters.depth: One-way ANOVA model: X_ij = μ + τ_i + ε_ij, where μ is the overall mean, τ_i the effect of level i, and ε_ij independent normal errors with mean 0 and common variance σ². Sums of squares: SST = Σ(X_ij − X̄..)² total, SSB = Σ n_i(X̄_i − X̄..)² between groups, SSE = Σ(X_ij − X̄_i)² within groups. df: k − 1 between, N − k within, N − 1 total, where k is the number of groups and N the total number of observations. Mean squares: MSB = SSB/(k − 1), MSE = SSE/(N − k). F = MSB/MSE with df (k − 1, N − k). Two-way classification without replication has two factors, row and column effects; test each with F = MS_row/MSE and F = MS_column/MSE. Interaction needs replication and is covered only by a few universities. Some syllabi call SSB the treatment sum of squares.

figure.title: One-way ANOVA table
figure.aria: An ANOVA table with between, within and total rows and columns for sum of squares, degrees of freedom, mean square and F.

chapters.example: Three machines make rods. Four rod lengths (mm) per machine are: M1: 9, 10, 11, 10; M2: 11, 12, 13, 12; M3: 13, 14, 15, 14. Test equality of means at α = 0.05. Group means are 10, 12, 14; grand mean is 12. SSB = 4[(10−12)² + (12−12)² + (14−12)²] = 4[4 + 0 + 4] = 32. SSE = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. df between = 2, df within = 9. MSB = 16, MSE = 6/9 = 0.667. F = 16/0.667 = 24. The critical value is F(0.05, 2, 9) = 4.26. Since 24 > 4.26, reject equality of means.
chapters.trap: Use the correct df: k − 1 for between and N − k for within. Do not run repeated t-tests for three or more means; that inflates the type I error rate.
chapters.leave: Two-factor interaction, repeated measures and post-hoc comparisons are left to advanced courses; regression is in Unit 1.
